## Project Vision and Goals

This project set out to explore how quantum computing approaches the Max-Cut 
problem differently from classical methods. Using Google's Cirq library, I 
implemented the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) and compared 
it against brute force and greedy classical baselines across graphs ranging 
from 4 to 30 nodes.

My six measurable goals were: formulating Max-Cut as an Ising Hamiltonian, 
implementing QAOA in Cirq, simulating quantum circuits, building classical 
baselines, evaluating approximation ratios, and analyzing runtime scaling.

## Results

All six goals were achieved. Key findings from the scaling experiments:

| n  | Brute Force | Greedy Ratio | QAOA Ratio | BF Time     | QAOA Time   |
|----|-------------|--------------|------------|-------------|-------------|
| 4  | 10.350      | 1.000        | 1.000      | ~0.000s     | ~0.936s     |
| 10 | 45.770      | 0.839        | 0.959      | 0.001s      | ~2.054s     |
| 20 | 169.310     | 0.899        | 0.877      | 3.308s      | ~6.663s     |
| 25 | 255.040     | 0.844        | 0.894      | 157.235s    | ~81.803s    |
| 30 | 361.540     | 0.839        | 0.858      | 7058.681s   | ~6181.511s  |

QAOA consistently outperformed greedy on smaller graphs but both methods 
degraded at larger sizes, an expected consequence of p=1 circuit depth.

The most striking result was runtime scaling. At n=30, brute force took 
**118 minutes** while QAOA simulation took **~103 minutes**. Projecting forward, 
brute force would take ~43 years at n=50. On real quantum hardware, that same 
QAOA circuit would run in microseconds.

## Reflection

The hardest part was finding research that explained expected results without 
giving away the implementation. Significant work constraints — four week-long 
field projects and a two-week remote dam maintenance assignment — made data 
collection difficult. The unexpected passing of my last close grandparent added 
further challenge during the project period.

The most surprising finding was QAOA occasionally losing to greedy. This turned 
out to be expected behavior at p=1 under classical simulation constraints and is 
not a flaw in the implementation.

## What's Next

Given more time I would run circuits on real quantum hardware via IBM Quantum, 
implement higher p values to show quality improvement with circuit depth, and 
benchmark against the Goemans-Williamson semidefinite programming approach.
